title: Why Humans Are Not Just Material

passages.text: The question: Can a wholly physical account explain conscious experience, individual selfhood, and our ability to understand reasons and values? What grounds Madhyasth Darshan’s proposal that their bearer is jeevan?

A human being can be well fed and still feel that life lacks meaning. We experience, question, judge, and seek understanding. The question is whether these are fully explained by the organisation of body, brain, and social life, or whether sentience is a further reality that such an account must recognise. This study develops reasons for the latter view while examining the strongest replies to it.

To say that humans are just material, in the sense examined here, is to say that their experience and thought belong entirely to the organised physical and chemical life of the person. It does not mean merely food, possessions, or concern for bodily comfort. A physicalist can recognise love, reasoning, and moral commitment as real features of an embodied person. The disagreement concerns what makes those features possible and whether a physical account is sufficient to explain them.

Three representative answers guide the inquiry: Madhyasth Darshan, which affirms body and a real sentient jeevan together; a physicalist interpretation of modern science; and Advaita Vedanta, which identifies the deepest Self with non-dual consciousness. The argument for sentience beyond a wholly physical account is kept distinct from the further claims that its bearer is an individual unit, that it has a particular atomic constitution, and that it persists after death.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan Answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that a human is the joint form of body and jeevan: an insentient body together with a real sentient self. The body provides the means of sensing and acting; jeevan experiences, evaluates, understands, and directs its participation in the world. Human fulfilment therefore concerns both bodily provision and the understanding through which a person lives in relationships.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Existence is not just physicochemical matter, but all physical, chemical and jeevan entities are inseparably present in Omnipresence.” — MVD, The Alternative, point 7, p. 5

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This answer joins an account of lived experience to an account of nature. The experiential distinctions come first below; the claim that a constitutionally complete sentient unit bears them follows in §1.3.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 A fresh starting point

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Shri A. Nagraj argues that two inherited approaches left the human question unresolved. Matter-centred inquiry explained bodily processes without adequately understanding the person, while mystery-centred spiritual traditions placed decisive knowledge beyond ordinary articulation. This is his criticism of those approaches, rather than a neutral history of science or Indian philosophy. His alternative is to make existence, the sentient self, and humane conduct understandable through study and evident in living (MVD, The Alternative, points 1 and 5, pp. 3–4).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 The argument from experience

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The starting point is familiar experience: what satisfies us, what we seek, how we experience ourselves, and why justice matters. Madhyasth Darshan reads these together as expressions of jeevan. They establish questions an adequate account of the human must answer; the physicalist interpretation of the same experiences is developed in §2.2.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2.1 Bodily satisfaction and personal fulfilment

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: A meal answers hunger, but it does not settle a broken relationship or the knowledge that one has acted unjustly. Conversely, a person may endure discomfort while remaining content because they kept a promise or helped someone. Bodily well-being and personal fulfilment support each other, yet neither simply substitutes for the other. Madhyasth Darshan connects this distinction to the different requirements of body and jeevan:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Activities such as eating and sleeping serve the body’s needs, while values and evaluation serve jeevan’s purpose. Mere sustenance of the body does not equate to jeevan’s fulfilment.” — SB, Ch. 7, PDF p. 92

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Its six perspectives (drishti) explain the direction of evaluation. Pleasant–unpleasant, healthy–unhealthy, and profit–loss guide much ordinary activity. Justice, dharma, and truth extend evaluation to the fulfilment of relationships and participation in the wider order. Awakening brings the first three under the guidance of the latter three (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.12).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2.2 The aspiration for continuous fulfilment

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Food, rest, and sensory pleasure have occasions and limits. The human aspiration, as Madhyasth Darshan understands it, is for happiness that continues: a settled way of living rather than an endless succession of pleasant sensations. This aspiration is often pursued through comfort and accumulation, yet acquiring more does not necessarily resolve the uncertainty about how to live. Nagraj connects that search to jeevan and interprets human production beyond immediate bodily needs as another expression of its capacity (JV, pp. 24–25).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Art, mathematics, philosophy, and institutions illustrate how human activity extends beyond immediate subsistence. Other animals also produce, learn, and transmit practices; the comparison concerns how these capacities are organised and extended (§2.3.4). Within Madhyasth Darshan, the positive answer to the search for fulfilment is four jeevan values: happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss. These name harmonies among its faculties, progressively joining hope, thought, desire, resolve, and realisation. Fulfilment is therefore a quality of the sentient self’s activity and relationships, rather than a quantity of goods consumed (JV, p. 137; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.8).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2.3 The experienced self and the changing body

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: We can attend to bodily pain, ageing, or fatigue while also reflecting on what these changes mean for us. We can distinguish the body we evaluate from ourselves as the one evaluating it. Madhyasth Darshan develops this distinction into its account of jeevan: the sentient self acts through a changing body while retaining its own constitution. Identifying oneself wholly with the body is therefore described as delusion (SB, PDF pp. 91–92).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The same account underlies the statement that jeevan does not sleep. Sleep belongs to the bodily medium, while the sentient unit continues its activity (SB, PDF p. 92). How this claim relates to experience and recall during sleep is examined in §2.2.3.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2.4 Justice as an inherent human orientation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that the human being seeks justice, wishes to act correctly, and is oriented towards truth from birth. Appropriate education and relationships develop this orientation into the capacity to give justice and recognise truth (SB, Ch. 1, PDF p. 15). On this account, teaching does more than install social preferences: it helps a person recognise and fulfil what relationships require.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The claim gives a direction to human development: justice can be understood and fulfilled, rather than reduced to whichever preference happens to prevail. How early social attention develops into a recognised obligation is considered in §2.2.4.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: These four observations support a distinction between bodily maintenance and the wider life of a person. The further step to jeevan depends on a stronger premise: bodily organisation cannot itself be the bearer of experience, aspiration, understanding, and evaluation. That premise needs its own defence. The distinction between functions does not alone establish distinct entities; §§2 and 5 examine the competing explanations.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 The account of what exists

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan places the sentient self within a real and perpetual nature. Its account connects the orders of nature, development in the atom, the body–jeevan joint form, and the human possibility of awakening.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.1 The four orders of nature

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Nature is described through four orders: material, biological, animal, and knowledge. Each is distinguished by characteristic activity, essential nature, and dharma. Material constituents compose biological forms, and biological cells compose animal and human bodies. In the animal order, a sentient unit works through a body with the hope to live. In the human or knowledge order, the same kind of unit can understand, evaluate, and responsibly participate in the other orders. Happiness is the human dharma; fortitude, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion characterise humane conduct (SB, PDF pp. 55, 179–180; MVD, p. 115).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Two developments must remain distinct. Compositional progression provides bodies and their environments. Development in an insentient atom reaches the sentient status called jeevan. Increasing bodily complexity is therefore not itself the production of sentience in this account (The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.5–1.6).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.2 The transition to sentient jeevan

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Constitutional completeness (gathanpurnata) means that an evolving atom has incorporated the particles required for its constitution and no longer gains or loses them. The texts describe an irreversible transition: the atom becomes free from molecular-bondage and weight-bondage and enters hope-bondage. Its constitution remains stable while its sentient activities can develop from delusion towards awakening (MVD, p. 91; SB, PDF pp. 55, 92).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Jeevan is neither physical nor non-physical. It is a constitutionally complete atom and a sentient entity.” — JV, p. 36

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This transition belongs to the darshan’s account of development within nature. The question of how constitutional completeness could be independently established is considered in §5.1.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The continuing identity of jeevan after bodily death follows within Madhyasth Darshan from this closed constitution. Bodies form and decompose; the sentient unit persists and can work through another body. Conservation of quantity alone would not establish that survival: the additional claim is that this particular constitution cannot disintegrate (JV, pp. 19, 54; The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.14, 6.2.2).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.3 Body and self are not the same

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The joint form gives the body and jeevan different but connected roles. The body supplies sensory organs, the brain, movement, and the bodily conditions of expression. Jeevan is the sentient participant: it experiences, selects, evaluates, and understands through this medium. Sensation belongs to their joint activity: a body constructed without jeevan would not evidence sensitivity, let alone understanding (JV, pp. 36–37).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Sensitivity concerns experience and response through the body and senses; comprehension concerns understanding relationships, values, and order. Both involve jeevan. Awakening brings them into balance by guiding sensory activity through understanding (SB, PDF p. 64). Bodily impairment constrains expression through the medium; delusion concerns how the already-present sentient self identifies and directs itself (The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.7, 6.2.2).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.4 Knowledge in the human order

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The human body provides the developed nervous system through which jeevan can understand existence and make that understanding evident. The unfolding of knowledge (gyan udghatan) occurs through the awakened human joint form. The knower is jeevan; the body supplies its means of expression (MVD, pp. 93, 115–116).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The brain (medhas) is described as receiving and processing signals associated with jeevan’s hopes, thoughts, desires, resolves, and authenticity, with bodily processes responding to them (MVD, pp. 83–84). This gives the brain a substantial role in the source account. The unresolved question is what measurable relation connects this description to neural activity, including the effects of injury and stimulation (§§2.3.3, 5.1; The Epistemology of Coexistence §7.3).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.5 The wisdom layer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan also uses kosha vocabulary for the capacities expressed across nature’s orders. In awakened humans, vigyanmaya names the opening of knowledge, wisdom, and science, through which the causes of unhappiness and their resolution become understandable (MVD, pp. 49–50). These are capacities expressed through the developing joint form. The five enduring faculties within jeevan — mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi, and atma — belong to a different part of the account. Advaita’s five sheaths also serve a different purpose (§3.2.4; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.7).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 The proposed test

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Understanding is fulfilled in living. Madhyasth Darshan asks a person to study existence, jeevan, and humane conduct; examine the proposal in their own experience; and make the understanding evident in relationships, work, and participation. Its evidence chain is Realisation – Behaviour – Experiment. Realisation must become resolution, work, conduct, and an awakened human tradition (MVD, p. 12).

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Authenticity (pramanikta) includes the ability to convey that understanding to another. Nagraj connects confidence in his understanding with its examination in living, fulfilment of responsibilities, and transmission to others (JV, pp. 25–27). This makes conduct and teaching integral to the proposal’s test. Whether these outcomes also establish its particular account of the sentient atom is a separate question addressed in §5.4.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.5 What makes this answer distinctive

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan affirms a real world in which many enduring sentient selves participate through bodies. Its account joins individuality to relationship, and understanding to responsible conduct. Human fulfilment comes through awakening in this world. Its distinctive claim is that the sentient participant is a constitutionally complete unit, irreducible to the organisation of its bodily medium.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Modern science studies human beings as evolved organisms whose mental lives depend on brains, bodies, relationships, and culture. Physicalism interprets this dependence as evidence that the organised person is sufficient to bear experience and thought. This need not mean that a useful account of love or justice can be replaced by a description of particles. The stronger claim is that these capacities require no sentient entity beyond the embodied person. Scientific findings constrain this interpretation without making it the only possible one.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.1 What science establishes — and what it does not

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Changes to the brain can alter particular experiences and motivations. The evidence includes interventions, such as stimulation, as well as observations of injury and development. A theory of the human must explain these detailed relationships, including why some capacities change while others remain. Establishing dependence, however, differs from establishing that experience is identical with neural activity.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: What a person can express also differs from what they can experience. Bodien et al. (2024) studied 353 adults with severe brain injuries. Among 241 who showed no observable command-following, 60 followed instructions through patterns detected by brain imaging or electrical recordings. Their cognition was discovered through brain activity despite its lack of outward expression. The sample does not establish how common this is in every clinical population, but it rules out treating absent movement as sufficient evidence of absent experience. Conversely, it supplies no evidence of cognition without a functioning brain.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.2 The physicalist reading of experience

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Physicalists can accept the experiences described in §1.2 while disputing what follows from them. The issue is whether differences within experience require different kinds of entity, or whether one embodied person can have bodily needs, lasting commitments, and awareness of both (Dennett 1991; Churchland 1986).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.2.1 Different fulfilments remain embodied

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: A physicalist account need not identify flourishing with bodily maintenance. Relationships, social learning, and reflection develop forms of fulfilment that cannot be replaced by food or comfort. Their difference from hunger does not place them beyond bodily organisation.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Neural injury makes this question concrete. Lockwood et al. (2024) compared 25 people with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a region involved in valuation, with groups who had other brain injuries or no injury. The affected group were less willing to exert effort for another person’s benefit, while effort for their own benefit was relatively preserved. This was a selective difference in motivation, not simply an inability to move. The task does not measure all morality, and the finding does not disprove a jeevan acting through an impaired medium. It does require that account to explain why a particular injury affects the willingness to help (§1.3.3).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.2.2 Unlimited wanting has naturalistic explanations

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Recurring desire need not imply an unlimited entity. Organisms must keep meeting changing needs, while learning and culture create goals that extend far beyond immediate survival. A person can also seek a settled life while continuing to need food and action within it. Continuous aspiration and endless acquisition should therefore be distinguished.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Active inference offers one candidate explanation of ongoing pursuit. It models choices through both preferred outcomes and opportunities to learn about the world (Friston et al. 2015). This helps explain why achieving one goal need not end activity. It does not establish that the aspiration for continuous happiness is merely biological regulation, or supply a complete theory of fulfilment. It gives the physicalist a possible account to develop alongside Madhyasth Darshan’s interpretation (§1.2.2).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.2.3 The felt self can be modelled as embodied

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: The sense of owning a body, being located somewhere, remembering one’s past, and remaining the same person are related but distinguishable. Lyu et al. (2023) found that stimulation of particular sites in the anterior precuneus, toward the back of the brain, changed bodily and spatial self-experience in nine patients. The felt relationship between self and body is therefore itself sensitive to neural intervention. This concerns particular aspects of selfhood, not the complete explanation of a subject.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Dreaming also occurs in an active brain. The DREAM database brings together 2,643 awakenings from 505 participants and relates reports of experience to preceding electrical brain activity (Wong et al. 2025). Dreams occur in both rapid-eye-movement and non-REM sleep. The research distinguishes reports of experience, experience whose contents cannot be recalled, and no experience; even the last may reflect failed recall. Dreaming during bodily immobility does not establish independence from neural activity. The claim that jeevan does not sleep must consequently distinguish continuous experience from a continuing capacity or bearer (§1.2.3).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.2.4 Early social attention and moral development

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Human social responsiveness begins early, but its interpretation needs care. Geraci et al. (2025) found that newborns around five days old looked longer at helpful or approaching interactions than at hindering or avoiding ones, with controls for non-social movement. This supports early sensitivity to social interactions. It does not show that newborns understand justice or already possess a moral doctrine.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: The evidence also varies across tasks. A coordinated study across 37 laboratories did not reproduce the expected preference for helpers in its tested sample of older infants (Lucca et al. 2025). Different ages, displays, and responses mean that this is not a direct refutation of the newborn finding. Together, the studies require distinctions between attention, preference, fairness expectations, and explicit obligation. Naturalistic accounts can allow early capacities that develop through experience. Their early appearance alone does not identify a separate bearer (§1.2.4; Ethics-And-Morals-In-Human-Beings).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3 The physicalist account of what exists

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Physicalism reads these findings as evidence for capacities belonging to an organised living being. Its replies to §1.3 concern how those capacities arise, why they vary, and what explanatory work a further entity would perform.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3.1 Evolution and the four orders

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Evolution describes branching relationships and changes in organisation rather than four separate ontological orders. This does not prevent meaningful distinctions between living and non-living systems or between different cognitive abilities. It asks how such distinctions arise and what evidence supports their boundaries. The existence of animals with complex capacities is already compatible with Madhyasth Darshan’s attribution of jeevan to animals. The disputed step is its separate atomic development into sentience, for which the study offers no independently identified physical transition (§1.3.2).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3.2 Mind emerges from organisation

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Physicalists take the organised brain and body, rather than their constituent matter considered separately, to realise mental capacities. Matter remains after the irreversible destruction of brain organisation, while no continuing personal capacities are publicly established. The physicalist concludes that the person does not survive. This is an interpretation of the dependence evidence, not an observation of a subject’s disappearance. Reversible loss of circulation or behavioural response must also be distinguished from irreversible brain destruction when assessing claims about death (§5.1).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3.3 Parsimony and the interaction challenge

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Calling the brain a medium accommodates dependence without explaining its particular form. A damaged instrument could obstruct expression, but the account must explain selective changes in motivation and self-experience, not only impaired movement. Such findings do not logically refute the medium proposal. They favour neural explanations insofar as those explanations predict the pattern while the added entity supplies no further prediction. Physicalists therefore ask what jeevan explains that the embodied account cannot.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: There is also a causal question. If every physical event has a sufficient physical cause, how does a distinct jeevan contribute to an action? Kim’s exclusion argument presses the alternatives of identifying the mental cause with the physical process, accepting two sufficient causes, or denying the additional cause any physical effect (Kim 2005). Madhyasth Darshan could challenge that starting assumption, but would then need to explain the relation it proposes. Conservation of energy alone does not establish physical causal closure, and a non-reductive account need not introduce extra energy. The unresolved issue is what the joint-form relation changes and how that change could be assessed (§1.3.4; The Epistemology of Coexistence §7.3).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3.4 Cognition, culture, and the brain

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Language and cumulative culture allow people to inherit achievements they could not recreate alone (Tomasello 2014). Some ingredients have wider roots: bumblebees learned a two-step puzzle from trained demonstrators that control bees did not independently solve under the tested conditions (Bridges et al. 2024). This demonstrates a form of social learning, not human reflective knowledge in an insect. It encourages precise comparisons rather than an absolute opposition between animal instinct and human understanding. A physicalist interprets human distinctiveness through developed capacities and cultural history; Madhyasth Darshan must show why those resources leave the knowledge order’s activity unexplained (§1.3.4).

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.3.5 Layered function, not koshas

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Neuroscience distinguishes interacting sensory, emotional, and cognitive functions without assigning them to koshas or a separate wisdom-bearing unit (Kandel et al. 2021). Similarities with the developmental envelopes described in §1.3.5 may help comparison, but do not establish a shared anatomy. Nor does identifying neural conditions of understanding decide whether its content is true or its use wise.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.4 Publicly controlled evidence

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: First-person reports are part of scientific inquiry: dream research could not identify its target without them. Public checking adds comparisons, independent analysis, and procedures that can expose mistaken interpretations. Specifying an expected result before collecting data helps prevent every outcome from being counted as support.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: The 2025 COGITATE collaboration used this approach to test competing predictions of integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory in 256 participants. Some predictions gained support and others were challenged, including predictions about sustained communication between regions at the back of the brain and responses when a stimulus disappeared. These results leave substantial questions open without showing that neural explanation as a whole has failed (Cogitate Consortium 2025). The same discipline can strengthen §1.4’s proposed verification: an account must allow outcomes that would count against its interpretation, even when its practices remain valuable.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: 2.5 What science leaves open

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: Explaining when experience occurs and what changes it leaves the disputed question of why those processes are experienced at all. Philosophers disagree over whether this hard problem requires a different account of what exists or a better understanding of how we know and describe experience (Chalmers 1995; Dennett 1991). The arguments are examined in §4.

passages.heading: 2-scientific-evidence-and-the-physicalist-answer
passages.section: 2. Scientific Evidence and the Physicalist Answer
passages.text: The alternatives also extend beyond the three positions compared here. Non-reductive physicalism allows psychological explanations their own importance while affirming physical constitution. Embodied and enactive approaches study cognition through a living being’s engagement with its surroundings; they need not reject physicalism. Russellian monism asks whether experience reveals aspects of reality left unspecified by physics’ account of structure and relations. Panpsychist versions place basic experiential properties more widely in nature (Strawson 2006; Goff 2019). None thereby establishes Madhyasth Darshan’s individual immortal unit. These alternatives show why an objection to one form of reduction does not settle the choice of ontology. Every proposal still owes an account of experience consistent with the detailed evidence about its bodily conditions.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3. The Advaita Vedanta Answer

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta holds that consciousness is the deepest reality of the human being. The true Self (Atman) is identical with Brahman, the one reality on which the world depends. Body, thought, desire, and the sense of being a separate person all belong to experience, but none is the final Self. The human is therefore not merely material; at the deepest level, the apparent division between a conscious person and an independent material world gives way to non-duality.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.1 A different starting point

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita begins with awareness as the condition of every experience. We can question what we perceive, remember, or believe, but those questions themselves occur in awareness. The inquiry turns from the changing contents of experience towards that through which they are known. This is witness-consciousness: the awareness in which bodily sensations, thoughts, and the feeling of being an individual appear (DDV, vv. 1–5).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The witness is not another thinker hidden behind the ordinary mind. Thinking, choosing, and wanting are themselves known. Advaita therefore takes the inquiry beyond the active inner self that Madhyasth Darshan affirms as jeevan. The distinction matters: the two traditions resist a body-only account, but they do not mean the same thing by the Self.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.2 The argument from experience

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita joins the Upanishadic neti neti (“not this, not this”) with the distinction between the seer and the seen. Whatever appears as an object of awareness can be examined and distinguished from awareness itself. The inquiry proceeds through body, sensation, thought, and ego, rather than stopping at the familiar feeling of “I” (BU 2.3.6; DDV, vv. 1–5).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.2.1 Two kinds of fulfilment are witnessed, not the Self

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The relief of hunger and the contentment of acting well differ in experience. Advaita accepts the distinction, while observing that both are known: bodily relief arises and passes, and so does the satisfaction following a just action. Neither changing state exhausts the awareness through which it is experienced. The inquiry therefore continues beyond both bodily satisfaction and the felt fulfilment of a person (DDV, vv. 1–5).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.2.2 Unlimited wanting is witnessed; the witness does not want

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Desire can return after a bodily need has been met. Advaita places this wanting, together with planning and the search for lasting happiness, within the changing life of the mind. Awareness knows the presence of desire and its absence. It is not itself a desire that must be satisfied. The distinction directs the seeker towards freedom from mistaken identification with the movements of mind (DDV, vv. 1–5).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.2.3 Awareness across waking, dreaming, and deep sleep

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Mandukya Upanishad examines waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Waking experience concerns the outward world; dreaming presents an inwardly experienced world; deep sleep is described through prajna, in which differentiated objects are not cognised and ignorance remains. Advaita reads these changing conditions in relation to a Self that none of them exhausts (MU, vv. 3–7).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The waking judgement that one slept peacefully forms part of this account of continuity. It needs to be distinguished from a detailed memory of what occurred during sleep. The further interpretation of such reports is considered alongside sleep research in §2.2.3 and the distinction between experienced unity and personal continuity in §4.3. Turiya names the non-dual Self that is not exhausted by waking, dreaming, or deep sleep. It is not a fourth blank interval added after the other three.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.2.4 Moral preparation and the five sheaths

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Truthfulness, self-control, and responsible conduct prepare the seeker for knowledge. They have force within everyday life, called vyavahara. Advaita does not dismiss them because they are not the final reality. Its inquiry asks the seeker to distinguish the Self from what changes, while living with the discipline needed for that inquiry (TU 1.11; VC, vv. 16–30).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The Taittiriya Upanishad moves inward through food-body, vitality, mind, intellect, and bliss. Advaita develops these as the five sheaths: annamaya, pranamaya, manomaya, vijnanamaya, and anandamaya. Each is examined in the search for the Self (TU 2.1–2.5; VC, vv. 154–212). These sheaths differ from both Madhyasth Darshan’s developmental envelopes and its faculties within jeevan (§1.3.5).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.3 The account of what exists

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita connects this inquiry into experience with its account of reality. Witness-consciousness is understood as Atman, and Atman as Brahman. The connection rests on the wider reasoning of the tradition and the Upanishads, not on the seer–seen distinction taken alone.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.3.1 Brahman alone is real; the world is appearance

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita holds that Brahman alone is ultimately real, while the world is mithya: dependent for its reality on Brahman, with its apparent independence overcome through knowledge. The world is neither wholly independent nor sheer non-being. Bodies, relationships, inquiry, causation, and conduct remain meaningful within ordinary experience. What is questioned is their apparent independence from Brahman (VC, v. 20; BSB, Adhyasa Bhashya).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: This distinction between everyday and ultimate reality prevents mithya from being reduced to “nothing exists” or “nothing matters.” Advaita’s claim concerns what the world ultimately is, even while people act, learn, and bear responsibility within it.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.3.2 You are not the body — or the mind

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Body, senses, thought, and the feeling of being “me” can each become objects of awareness. Advaita reasons that none can therefore be the final seer. It identifies that seer as the Self that was never born and does not die (DDV, vv. 1–5; KU 1.2.18; BG 2.20). The conclusion reaches beyond ordinary personal identity: the changing mind and its history are also distinguished from Atman. Whether the seer–seen distinction warrants these conclusions is examined in §5.3.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.3.3 The self is not individual; the question dissolves

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The apparent separate person (jiva) arises through ignorance (avidya): self and not-self are confused, and the properties of one are attributed to the other. Advaita calls this superimposition (adhyasa). Liberation (moksha) is the removal of this mistake through knowledge. The Self does not become Brahman; it is recognised as having always been Brahman, one without a second (BSB, Adhyasa Bhashya; CU 6.2.1, 6.8.7).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: From this standpoint, the question “Is the human just material?” contains an assumption that must itself be examined: that a separate human stands within an independently existing material world. Advaita holds that the distinction is valid in ordinary life but does not describe ultimate reality. Both the person and the world depend on Brahman.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.4 Scripture, reason, and meditation

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: The classical path joins hearing the teaching (shravana), reasoning over it (manana), and sustained contemplation (nididhyasana), under a qualified teacher (BU 2.4.5). Reason is used to examine doubts and apparent contradictions; contemplation addresses habitual identification with body and mind. Scripture is treated as a means of knowing the Self where ordinary perception cannot make it an object.

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: This is a substantive claim about how knowledge is possible. Advaita asks the seeker to understand and realise the teaching, while granting the Upanishads an authority that a physicalist or a student of Madhyasth Darshan need not accept. The comparative question is how the method distinguishes genuine understanding from conviction shaped by its starting assumptions (§5.3).

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: 3.5 What makes this answer distinctive

passages.heading: 3-the-advaita-vedanta-answer
passages.text: Advaita locates the final Self in unchanging awareness, beyond the active individual mind. Madhyasth Darshan gives lasting reality to individual jeevan units and to the world in which they live. Advaita gives persons and relationships their place within everyday reality, while denying that they remain ultimately separate. Their shared resistance to a body-only account therefore leads to different understandings of individuality, knowledge, and liberation.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4. Comparing the Three Views

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The three positions differ over what experience reveals, what a human being is, and how those claims can be assessed. Scientific findings constrain every account of embodied life. Physicalism draws a further conclusion about what those findings mean for the nature of mind.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Question Physicalist interpretation Madhyasth Darshan Advaita Vedanta What is a human? An embodied organism whose mental life is physically realised and socially developed Body and jeevan acting together Ultimately Atman = Brahman; the separate person belongs to everyday experience Is the world real? Yes; physical reality is sufficient to account for it Yes; nature and its sentient units are real and perpetual The world is mithya: meaningful in experience, without final independent reality What is consciousness? passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4.1 The central differences

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: For Madhyasth Darshan, both the world and individual sentient selves are fully real. This allows relationships, understanding, and responsible conduct to retain their place in the account of existence. Advaita gives them their place within everyday reality but holds that their apparent separateness is overcome in knowledge of Brahman. Physicalism treats the embodied person as sufficient for experience and action, while asking how capacities develop through biological and social life.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s position between these two answers is not the origin of its name. Madhyasth refers to the mediative or regulative role through which Omnipresence and atomic nuclei sustain order (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.11). Its affirmation of a perpetual world and many distinct jeevan units must be understood through that account, rather than as a compromise between materialism and Advaita.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The traditions also differ over the reach of their methods. First-person examination can reveal distinctions within experience. Public experiments can identify conditions on which reported experience and action depend. Reasoning can examine whether a proposed explanation follows from its premises. Conduct can show whether an understanding is lived and conveyed. The question is how these kinds of evidence support one another without allowing success in one domain to settle every claim in another.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Further comparisons, including Buddhist accounts that deny a permanent self, help separate rejection of material reduction from affirmation of an immortal individual. The wider range is considered in The Ontology of Coexistence §5. The following questions bring the central disagreement into focus.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4.2 What a physical description tells us about experience

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The strongest reason for questioning a wholly material account concerns the presence of experience itself. A description of pain can explain the detection of injury, the transmission of signals, withdrawal, learning, and a person’s report. The further question is why any of these processes should hurt. Explaining their contribution to survival does not yet explain their felt character. Madhyasth Darshan locates that character in a sentient knower; Advaita starts from awareness; the physicalist identifies it with an activity of the organism.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The knowledge argument makes the disagreement vivid. Imagine someone who knows every physical fact about colour vision but has never experienced colour. On seeing red, would this person learn something about what red looks like? If so, and if what is learned is a fact absent from complete physical knowledge, physical facts would not exhaust the facts about experience. The argument’s force lies in the difference between describing experience and knowing it through undergoing it (Chalmers 2003).

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The physicalist disputes the inference. Someone can acquire a new way of recognising or thinking about a state without discovering a second kind of reality. First-person acquaintance and a scientific description may concern the same state, just as different descriptions can identify the same person. The analogy illustrates the reply without establishing the proposed identity between experience and brain activity. Papineau develops this reply through the distinction between concepts acquired through experience and concepts used in physical explanation (Papineau 2020). The question is whether the new understanding reveals something additional in reality or a new way of knowing what was already described.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: This study gives weight to the first possibility. An explanation should account for the experienced character of pain as well as the work pain does. That is a reason to question the sufficiency of a description confined to structure and function. To establish that physicalism is false, the argument must show why the proposed identity cannot account for this difference; the present explanatory difficulty alone does not establish that failure.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4.3 Why experience belongs together

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Experience also has a unity that demands explanation. When someone listens to a friend, the voice, the expression on the friend’s face, and the listener’s concern can occur together within one experience. Explaining how information is coordinated for action addresses part of this phenomenon. It remains possible to ask why the coordinated processes are experienced together by a subject.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Bayne and Chalmers distinguish this experienced unity from the ability to combine information in thought or report. Their argument challenges theories that explain separate conscious states without explaining their belonging to a common experience (Bayne and Chalmers 2003). Madhyasth Darshan’s single jeevan offers a definite bearer of that unity. This is an attraction of the proposal: it starts with a sentient individual rather than attempting to assemble one subject out of many already separate subjects.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: A physicalist can nevertheless hold that a unified experience is realised by coordinated activity distributed through an organism. Unity in experience does not by itself require a spatial point at which everything converges. Nor does it establish an indivisible atom or an enduring identity after death. The competing accounts must explain the kinds of unity that remain, and the kinds that change, when neural connections are altered (§2.3.3). Madhyasth Darshan’s proposal still needs to explain how one jeevan receives and experiences the particular contents made available through that changing organisation.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Studies of people whose major connection between the brain’s hemispheres has been severed complicate a simple answer. Some information becomes difficult to compare across the two sides, yet findings from a two-patient study and a later one-patient study have been interpreted as preserving aspects of conscious unity (Pinto et al. 2017, 2023). These small samples and particular tasks do not settle how many subjects there are. They show why neither “two disconnected hemispheres mean two people” nor “one person proves an indivisible atom” follows directly from the evidence. The relation between neural coordination and experienced unity remains a question for both accounts.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4.4 Reasons, values, and the life of a knower

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: A complete account of the human must also explain understanding. A belief concerns something: a friend’s promise, yesterday’s event, or a mathematical relation. We assess it for truth and ask whether the reasons offered justify it. Similarly, a judgment about justice can be criticised even when it is popular or useful. Madhyasth Darshan’s account of the knowledge order gives these activities a central place in human life. Its attraction is the connection it draws between knowing, evaluating, and fulfilling relationships.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: The physicalist need not deny any of this. A process can have a physical explanation while also expressing a reason. Naturalistic theories of meaning seek to explain how representations concern things by examining their use in perception, action, learning, and communication. Papineau, for example, connects representational content with the biological functions of the processes that use it (Papineau 2016). Such accounts have to explain both successful understanding and mistakes; a mere sequence of physical causes does not tell us which belief is justified.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Evolutionary usefulness likewise gives no automatic guarantee of truth. Accurate beliefs often help organisms act successfully, while other beliefs may persist because they secure approval or protect group identity. Sterelny’s recent reconsideration of moral realism stresses this difficulty: his earlier defence had overestimated the extent to which the evolution of cooperation supported reliable moral judgment (Sterelny 2025). This leaves room for a serious challenge to explaining moral authority through social usefulness alone. It does not show that physically embodied minds cannot recognise valid reasons, or that only jeevan could do so. Madhyasth Darshan must explain how its account supports reliable understanding and how errors can be recognised and corrected.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: 4.5 From these considerations to jeevan

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: These arguments strengthen the case for taking experience and understanding as real features that an account of nature must explain. They support questioning a picture of human life exhausted by the workings of an insentient mechanism. Their connection with Madhyasth Darshan is therefore substantive: jeevan is proposed as the sentient individual whose experiencing, understanding, and evaluation become evident through the body.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Several further judgments are needed to accept that proposal. Human fulfilment exceeding bodily maintenance does not establish that experience exceeds every possible physical explanation. Even if experience is irreducible, it might belong to an organism, to a fundamental aspect of nature, or to the universal awareness proposed by Advaita. Identifying a distinct individual bearer would still leave its constitution and persistence to be established. The difference between bodily and personal fulfilment, the reality of experience, the unity of a subject, constitutional completeness, and survival are connected questions, but an answer to one cannot serve as the evidence for all the others.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-the-three-views
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s value here lies in offering a connected account to examine. Its unity of consciousness, individuality, understanding, and responsibility gives reasons to pursue it. Comparison must establish whether those connections explain the evidence more fully than the alternatives and whether its distinctive claims can withstand independent criticism.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5. Critical Review

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The three accounts differ in explanatory ambition and in the evidence supporting their claims.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.1 Madhyasth Darshan — individual sentience in a shared world

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan connects a real world, individual experience, understanding, and responsibility. Its account of fulfilment gives relationships and humane conduct a place within its explanation of what a human is.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: A single sentient jeevan provides a proposed bearer of experienced unity and agency. It avoids combining many already distinct subjects, while retaining enduring individuality in contrast with Advaita’s final account.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Its demand that understanding become evident in work, conduct, and transmission creates an opportunity for public comparison when outcomes and conditions of success are clearly stated.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The transition to sentience needs independent support. Constitutional completeness is a definite source claim, but its publicly identifiable conditions remain unspecified. The account must also explain why closing an insentient atom’s constitution should bring experience into existence. Describing that experience as previously latent would leave the connection to be explained (The Ontology of Coexistence §6.2.1).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The bodily medium needs a more exact account. The joint form allows bodily impairment to constrain expression. It must also explain why particular neural changes affect particular aspects of motivation, memory, and self-experience. Calling the brain an instrument leaves this detailed relation to be explained (§2.3.3; The Ontology of Coexistence §6.2.2).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Persistence requires its own evidence. Neither experienced unity nor conservation establishes an immortal person. Temporary circulatory arrest and irreversible brain destruction are different conditions. In a prospective surgical study, some patients recalled experiences and some guessed presented words, but none explicitly recalled the experimental targets. Chance could not be excluded for the guesses. Experience timing was uncertain, and recordings could not establish that the reported experiences occurred without brain activity. This was no demonstration of post-death survival (Ross et al. 2025).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Practical verification needs protection against circularity. Agreement with a teacher cannot itself establish realisation. Assessment must allow disagreement, failed outcomes, and ethical conduct under rival philosophies. Even independently demonstrated practical benefit would support the tested conduct claims, while the proposed atom would still require separate evidence (The Ontology of Coexistence §6.2.3).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan offers a coherent direction for investigating individual sentience, but its particular bearer, bodily relation, and persistence remain claims to establish.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.2 Physicalism — strong bodily explanations, disputed completeness

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Physicalism draws support from the detailed dependence of human capacities on an evolved brain, body, and social world. The interventions and comparisons in §2 give this support greater force than correlation alone.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: It can recognise meaning, personal fulfilment, and moral reasoning without adding another entity, while retaining psychological and social explanations of physically realised capacities.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The scientific explanations it draws on can be independently tested and corrected. These methods provide strong constraints on every account of the human, including Madhyasth Darshan.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Bodily explanation has not settled the nature of experience. Explaining a person’s responses and reports leaves the dispute in §4.2: whether the experience is fully accounted for or whether something essential remains outside that description. Replies based on different ways of knowing the same state must be assessed as arguments.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Introspection needs explanation rather than blanket acceptance or dismissal. A physicalist may explain why experience seems irreducible through the brain’s simplified representations of its own activity. It must show how those representations arise and why the proposed correction is warranted (Graziano 2024).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Success cannot make the method itself a proof of physicalism. Science does not have to assume that it detects only matter. A claimed additional cause can be investigated through its effects. The existence of complete physical explanations for everything remains a stronger claim than the success of the explanations presently available.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: A history of values is not their full justification. Explaining how a judgment arose does not by itself show that it is true or binding. Naturalistic ethics has serious resources for this task, but its conclusions require argument (§4.4).

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Physicalism remains a powerful interpretation of the evidence, while its claim to exhaust experience and understanding faces substantive philosophical objections.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.3 Advaita Vedanta — awareness and the limits of individuality

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Strengths.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita gives awareness a foundational place and examines the identification of the self with changing bodily and mental states. Its disciplined inquiry treats the first-person character of experience as central.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Its non-dual account seeks to understand apparent plurality through one ultimate reality, while preserving inquiry and ethical obligations within ordinary life.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Weaknesses.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The observer argument needs qualification. The fact that a body or thought can be observed does not establish that an embodied organism cannot observe itself. Advaita must answer that alternative as well as distinguish awareness from particular experienced contents.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Universal identity requires further warrant. Self-inquiry alone does not establish that all subjects are one Brahman, or that the world is mithya. Those claims depend on wider reasoning and the authority accorded to Upanishadic testimony.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Dependent appearance remains difficult to explain. Advaita must account for ignorance and plurality without granting them the independent reality it denies. Its schools differ over how this is done.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: The final significance of relationship is disputed. Madhyasth Darshan’s objection concerns whether individual persons and relationships retain ultimate significance when their separateness is overcome in knowledge; it does not deny Advaita’s teaching of humane conduct.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Advaita offers a substantial challenge to bodily identification, while its universal conclusion requires commitments beyond the immediate presence of awareness.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: 5.4 Where the argument leads

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: This study favours the view that humans are not exhausted by insentient physicochemical organisation. Its reason is the apparent difference between what a process does and what it is like to undergo it: even a complete description of the first seems to leave the second unexplained. Unity, understanding, and evaluation give further substance to the question of the sentient knower. The physicalist reply that these are different ways of knowing the same reality remains a serious challenge to this judgment.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan is a promising account within that broader judgment because it joins individual sentience with a real world and responsibility in relationships. This gives reasons to investigate jeevan; it does not establish constitutional completeness or immortality. Confidence in those further claims should depend on evidence that can distinguish them from competing explanations. A reproducible relation between the proposed unit and neural activity would matter to the bodily account. Independent evidence of personal continuity would matter to survival. Carefully compared outcomes in conduct would matter to practical claims.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: A useful test must specify the expected result and what would count against the proposal before its outcome is known. For conduct, this means comparing clearly described practices and outcomes with credible alternatives, with assessment open to people who do not accept the philosophy. For the body–jeevan relation, an unexplained neural result would be a starting point for inquiry; identifying jeevan would require evidence for its particular properties. Success in one test cannot substitute for the others.

passages.heading: 5-critical-review
passages.text: Further success in explaining experience and understanding entirely through bodily organisation would strengthen physicalism. Evidence for an independently persisting sentient unit would strengthen Madhyasth Darshan. The present inclination therefore carries a continuing obligation: to develop the affirmative account, answer its strongest objections, and revise it wherever better reasons or evidence require.

passages.text: Appendix: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Key terms from §§1–5 are collected here for quick reference. Each term is also defined where it first appears in the exposition.

passages.heading: appendix-quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Jeevan The sentient self — in Shri A. Nagraj’s view a real, eternal, constitutionally complete unit that works through the body. It is neither brain activity nor an immaterial soul added from outside nature. For its ontology and conservation claims, see The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.6–1.8, 1.14, 6.2. Constitutional completeness (gathanpurnata) The claimed irreversible transition at which an evolving atom’s constitution closes and the unit becomes sentient jeevan. Developed in The Ontology of Coexistence §1.6.1. Coexistence (saha-astitva) Existence seen as all units inseparably present together. Knowledge order (gyan avastha) The human level of nature — able to know and evaluate every other level. Gyan udghatan Knowledge becoming clear and evident in thought and conduct through the awakened human joint form; jeevan is the knower and the body its medium (The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.1). Pramanikta Authenticity: understanding made evident in conduct, teaching, and humane tradition (The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.6). Rahasyata Mysteriousness: what remains unclear to the knower and can become understandable through inquiry (The Epistemology of Coexistence §§3.4, 7.1). Sensitivity / comprehension Experience and response through body and senses / understanding relationship, value, and order. Both involve jeevan in the joint form (The Epistemology of Coexistence §1.5). Six perspectives (drishti) Evaluative lenses in human behaviour — priya/hita/labh and humane nyaya/dharma/satya (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.12). Atman / *Brahman* In Advaita Vedanta: the innermost Self / the one ultimate reality. Advaita says they are identical. Mithya Advaita’s term for the world: not absolutely real, a dependent appearance. Physicalism The view that everything about a person, including conscious experience, belongs to physical reality; this need not make psychological or social explanations dispensable. Irreducible experience Experience that cannot be fully accounted for by a description of physical structure and function. Whether this requires a distinct entity is a further question.

passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Source terms and their physical interpretation

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Constitutional completeness, molecular-bondage, and weight-bondage translate the source terms gathanpurnata, anu-bandhan, and bhar-bandhan. They belong to Madhyasth Darshan’s account of an insentient atom becoming sentient. Their use here does not identify a recognised particle, equate freedom from weight-bondage with zero rest mass, or establish a measured physical mechanism (MVD, p. 91). How these terms might connect to physical measurement remains open. The phrase “neither physical nor non-physical” also belongs to the darshan’s own classification of nature (JV, p. 36). If a sentient unit were independently identified, a further question would arise: whether it extends a physical account or supports a different understanding of nature.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Intelligibility and the transition to sentience

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Pervasive gyan and the sentience of jeevan have related but distinct roles in the source account. Existence is intelligible; the constitutionally complete unit is the knower. Describing their connection as “latency actualised” would add an interpretation: it would require showing why intelligibility entails a latent capacity for felt experience. The study therefore states the source’s irreversible transition positively without using that interpretation as its explanation (MVD, pp. 35, 91; SB, PDF pp. 48, 92).

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: MVD citations use its printed page labels, which match the PDF positions cited here. JV citations use printed English page numbers; the corresponding PDF position is one greater. SB citations explicitly identify one-based PDF positions. These conventions apply to the particular translations linked in References. The English translations remain open to refinement; MVD and SB identify themselves as working drafts.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Advaita texts and interpretive scope

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The Advaita account follows the translations and commentaries linked below, using their verse and section numbers. Vivekachudamani and Drig-Drishya-Viveka are cited as teaching texts within the tradition; their disputed authorship does not settle their arguments. Applications to the four experiences in §3.2 are comparative interpretations of these texts, rather than claims that the texts discuss the modern examples. The three states in the Mandukya Upanishad are presented through their Advaita interpretation.
